issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
Frank has been driving a delivery truck for forty years, and for most of that time, he believed he understood the world. It was a place of simple transactions: you delivered a package, you got a signature, you said "have a good one," and you moved on. That sense of order vanished six months ago on a Tuesday afternoon. The delivery was to a secluded house at the end of a winding dirt road. As he approached the door, two young men appeared from around the side of the house. There was no conversation, no demand, just a sudden, disorienting shove from behind. He remembers the sharp crack of his head against the doorframe and the rough texture of the gravel on his cheek. They took his wallet and the scanner from his belt and were gone in less than a minute, leaving him dizzy and bleeding on the porch of a stranger.

In the weeks that followed, Frank insisted he was fine. He took only two days off before getting back behind the wheel, a decision he now recognizes as the beginning of his new, exhausting routine. He began working hard at keeping busy, taking every extra shift he could, volunteering for the late-night runs nobody else wanted. At home, he filled his time with frantic activity-mowing the lawn twice a week, reorganizing the garage until there was nothing left to organize, fixing things that weren't broken. His wife, Martha, found him one night at 2 a.m. tightening the bolts on their kitchen chairs. He was trying to outrun his own mind. He had come to believe that his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed; the ground beneath his feet, once so solid, now felt unpredictable and treacherous.

The core of his struggle is a fear he cannot voice. Frank is certain that if he allows himself to think about the event in any detail, he will not be able to handle it. The thought itself feels like a threat, a promise of a collapse from which he might never recover. So he tries hard not to think about it. When a flash of memory comes-the glint of the sun off a belt buckle, the smell of pine needles from the surrounding woods-he shoves it down and immediately finds a task. When the busyness isn't enough, especially late at night when the house is still, he turns to food. He eats excessively, standing in the dim light of the open refrigerator, consuming leftovers without tasting them, seeking the dull, heavy comfort of a full stomach to quell the rising panic in his chest.

His job, once a source of pride and simple satisfaction, has become a landscape of potential threats. Every unfamiliar driveway, every shadowy porch, every customer who seems agitated or unpredictable sends a jolt of adrenaline through him. He doubts himself constantly, convinced he can't trust that he will do the right thing in a crisis. He replays the assault, not with clarity, but with a suffocating sense of failure. Why didn't he see them coming? Why didn't he say something different? This self-doubt paralyzes him, causing him to hesitate before knocking on a door or to take convoluted routes to avoid certain neighborhoods. His route times have suffered, and his supervisor has taken notice.

It was Martha who finally insisted he seek help. The constant busyness had erected a wall between them, and his refusal to speak about what happened had left her feeling helpless. She found him one evening sitting in his truck in their own driveway, engine off, staring at their front door for nearly an hour, unable to make the short walk to safety. He came to his first appointment looking worn down, not by his age, but by the immense, invisible effort of keeping his own thoughts at bay. He is terrified that talking about the assault will unleash the breakdown he has worked so hard to prevent, but a small part of him hopes it might be the only way to finally stop running.
